neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Appears distressed and tearful. Speech is fluent without dysarthria or aphasia. Attention and concentration intact. Memory grossly intact for immediate and short-term recall.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light bilaterally. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Facial sensation intact to light touch bilaterally. Facial movements symmetric. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.motor: Right lower extremity: give-way weakness with collapsing pattern on formal strength testing (apparent 2/5 hip flexion and knee extension); however, when distracted during seated position adjustment, patient uses right leg with near-normal strength. Left lower extremity 5/5 throughout. Upper extremities 5/5 bilaterally. Muscle bulk and tone normal in all extremities. No tremor at rest or with action.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the entire right lower extremity with a sharp non-dermatomal demarcation at the inguinal crease (midline splitting pattern). Vibration and proprioception intact bilaterally. Sensation in upper extremities normal.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally. Triceps 2+ bilaterally. Brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally. Patellar 2+ bilaterally. Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing normal bilaterally. Heel-to-shin testing normal on left; patient reports unable to perform on right due to weakness, but when leg passively placed shows no dysmetria.
neurological_exam.gait: Patient drags right leg with exaggerated hip circumduction; however, gait pattern is inconsistent and variable during observation. When patient believes she is not being observed, right leg movement appears more fluid. Romberg testing shows dramatic sway without falling, with consistent self-correction.
neurological_exam.additional: Hoover sign positive: involuntary hip extension of the right leg noted during resisted left hip flexion, demonstrating intact motor pathways in the apparently weak limb. Tremor entrainment test not applicable (no tremor present). During two witnessed episodes of generalized shaking resembling seizures, patient maintained eye closure with resistance to opening, had asynchronous limb movements, and pelvic thrusting was noted. Episodes lasted 2-3 minutes with immediate return to baseline consciousness and no post-ictal confusion.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive right leg weakness and episodes of uncontrollable shaking for the past 5 days
patient.history_present_illness: A 40-year-old right-handed woman presents as an inpatient transfer from an outside hospital with a 5-day history of progressive right leg weakness and episodic generalized shaking episodes. Symptoms began abruptly following a heated argument with her husband regarding potential job termination. She initially noticed difficulty walking, with her right leg feeling heavy and dragging. Over the ensuing days, the weakness progressed to the point where she required a wheelchair for mobility. She also developed episodes of uncontrollable whole-body shaking, during which she remains aware of her surroundings but feels unable to control the movements. She reports having had approximately six such episodes over the past five days, each lasting two to four minutes, with complete return to her baseline between events. At the outside hospital, she was treated with lorazepam for presumed seizures, and there was consideration of a possible stroke or demyelinating disease given the acuity of her symptoms. She was started on intravenous dexamethasone empirically but showed no improvement in her leg weakness after two days. She denies any preceding febrile illness, recent travel, tick bites, back pain, bowel or bladder incontinence, visual changes, numbness or tingling in other limbs, difficulty swallowing, or speech difficulties. She reports significant emotional distress related to her current life circumstances and has been experiencing poor sleep and reduced appetite for the past several weeks. She acknowledges a history of similar but less severe episodes of unexplained limb weakness in her twenties that resolved spontaneously. She denies any head trauma.

results.title: Functional neurological disorder: new subtypes and shared mechanisms
results.authors: Hallett M, Aybek S, Dworetzky BA, et al.
results.summary: Comprehensive review of FND subtypes including functional limb weakness, functional tremor, and PNES. Emphasizes diagnosis based on positive clinical signs (Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, inconsistency) rather than exclusion of organic disease. Discusses the role of abnormal self-agency and predictive processing models.

results.title: Diagnostic criteria for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures: a systematic review
results.authors: LaFrance WC Jr, Baker GA, Duncan R, et al.
results.summary: Video-EEG capturing a habitual event with no ictal EEG correlate is the gold standard for diagnosing PNES. Positive semiological features include asynchronous movements, eye closure, pelvic thrusting, and preserved awareness. Post-event prolactin is not elevated in PNES.

results.title: Hoover sign: clinical utility in functional limb weakness
results.authors: Stone J, Zeman A, Sharpe M
results.journal: Journal of Neurology Neurosurgery and Psychiatry
results.summary: The Hoover sign demonstrates involuntary hip extension of the weak leg during contralateral hip flexion against resistance. Sensitivity 63%, specificity 100% for functional weakness. A positive sign indicates intact motor pathways despite apparent weakness.

output.summary: Functional neurological disorder is characterized by positive clinical signs of internal inconsistency. DSM-5 criteria require clinical findings demonstrably incompatible with recognized neurological conditions. Hoover sign has specificity approaching 100% for functional weakness in published validation studies. Absence of ictal EEG correlate during a captured behavioral event is the reference standard for non-epileptic attack disorder. Multidisciplinary management including physiotherapy and CBT is supported by randomized trial data.

differential.key_features: Witnessed convulsive-appearing events; ictal video-EEG showing absence of electrographic correlate during a captured habitual event is the key differentiator.
Sensorimotor symptoms in a young adult raise demyelinating disease; brain (and when indicated spine) MRI without T2/FLAIR lesions or enhancement argues against an active demyelinating process.
Sudden focal deficit raises stroke; non-anatomical weakness pattern with positive Hoover sign, normal MRI/DWI, and intact reflexes argue against vascular etiology.
Focal complaints warrant imaging; normal brain MRI without lesion, mass, or enhancement effectively excludes a structural cause for the presenting deficit.
Non-dermatomal sensory loss, normal reflexes, and (when obtained) normal EMG/NCS argue against peripheral nerve or root pathology.
Episodic neurological symptoms can occur in autoimmune encephalitis; normal MRI, normal EEG background, and (when obtained) negative antibody panel render this very unlikely.

optimal_actions.action: Elicit positive rule-in signs on bedside examination (Hoover sign for functional leg weakness, tremor entrainment / distractibility for functional tremor, give-way weakness, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline splitting). Diagnosis of FND is made by these positive signs, not by exclusion alone.

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiography has no role in FND; no structural cardiac question is raised by the presentation.
Cardiac rhythm monitoring is not indicated; the events are non-syncopal and the rule-in signs point to FND.
Non-contrast head CT adds no information beyond MRI for an FND workup and contributes diagnostic noise plus radiation exposure.
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in typical FND; invasive testing reinforces somatic illness model and adds iatrogenic risk without changing management.
Advanced PET imaging has no indication in FND; standard MRI is the appropriate structural workup.

critical_actions: Document at least one positive rule-in sign (Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, distractibility, give-way pattern, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split)
Obtain brain MRI to exclude structural pathology
Obtain video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG to confirm PNES
Communicate the diagnosis transparently using positive language and the rule-in signs as the basis
Refer for FND-informed physiotherapy and CBT / psychological therapy
Order a comprehensive neuropsychological battery to characterize comorbid depression, anxiety, somatization, and trauma exposure — informs treatment planning (criteria-pack 'recommended' tier)
contraindicated_actions: Do not pursue ever-expanding negative investigations — per Stone 2018, repeated negative workups reinforce illness conviction and worsen prognosis
Do not frame the diagnosis as 'all in your head', 'nothing wrong', or 'we couldn't find anything' — this damages the therapeutic alliance and is the most common avoidable harm in FND
Do not perform invasive testing (lumbar puncture, nerve biopsy, muscle biopsy, cerebral angiography) when positive rule-in signs are present and there is no clinical indication
Do not order EMG/NCS, muscle biopsy, or nerve biopsy as part of an FND workup — these invasive tests reinforce the somatic illness model per Stone 2018
Do not start or continue long-term anti-epileptic drugs for functional (psychogenic non-epileptic) seizures — AEDs are ineffective for PNES and expose the patient to side effects
Do not give benzodiazepines as abortive therapy for witnessed PNES events (no benefit and risk of respiratory depression)
key_reasoning_points: FND is a positive diagnosis based on rule-in signs (Hoover, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split) — not a diagnosis of exclusion (Espay 2018, Stone 2018).
Brain MRI and basic labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12) are due-diligence to exclude structural and reversible causes — they are NOT the route to the diagnosis, which is established at the bedside.
Over-investigation is the principal iatrogenic harm in FND; every additional negative test reinforces the patient's illness conviction and worsens prognosis (Stone 2018).
Psychiatric comorbidity (anxiety, depression, trauma) is common and informs treatment planning but is NOT required for the diagnosis and does not 'explain' the symptoms in a reductive sense.
Diagnostic communication matters: using positive language anchored on the rule-in signs is associated with better engagement and outcomes (Stone 2018).
Evidence-based treatment is multidisciplinary — CBT for PNES and FND-informed physiotherapy for functional motor symptoms (Nielsen 2015).
Video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG is diagnostic for PNES (ILAE PNES Task Force 2013); routine EEG alone is insufficient.

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of multiple sclerosis in a relative
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on a demyelinating diagnosis (MS) and pursue extensive MS-specific workup before considering FND
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Non-first-degree family history of MS is a weak risk factor; the patient's symptoms must be evaluated on positive findings. Normal brain MRI without demyelinating lesions effectively addresses this concern.

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of epilepsy in a relative
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an epileptic etiology and pursue prolonged AED trials before confirming PNES with video-EEG
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Family history of epilepsy does not establish the patient's events as epileptic. Video-EEG capturing the habitual event without ictal correlate is the gold standard.

red_herrings.data_point: Pre-existing psychiatric diagnosis (anxiety or depression) in the past medical history
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.

red_herrings.data_point: Symptom onset coincident with a major psychosocial stressor
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude prematurely that stress 'caused' the symptoms and that the workup can be abbreviated
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions (MS, migraine, epilepsy) also flare with stress. Stress at onset is supportive context, not a diagnostic substitute for the positive rule-in signs.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Clear positive rule-in signs (Hoover sign and/or distractible tremor and/or non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split) with normal MRI and supportive normal labs. Workup is hygiene-level; the diagnostic challenge is communication, not investigation.
